newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: S.Lanka battle toll a sign rebels should quit-paper.
newsitem.headline: S.Lanka battle toll a sign rebels should quit-paper.

text.p: Sri Lanka's state media said on Monday that the high death toll in fighting with Tamil Tiger guerrillas in the northern Wanni region should set all sides thinking about the futility of the war, but analysts said the rebels would not give up easily.

"The news that well over 100 LTTE (Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam) cadres have lost their lives in Omanthai in a confrontation with security forces should set all parties to the conflict thinking," the state-owned Daily News said.

The Defence Ministry said more than 250 LTTE guerrillas and security force personnel were killed after the Tigers attacked the military's forward defences on Friday night near Omanthai, just north of the government-held town of Vavuniya, which lies some 220 km (135 miles) north of the capital Colombo.
The rebels said in a statement from their London office late on Sunday that 126 guerrillas had died in the battle.
The Daily News said the battle should remind the LTTE that they were in a no-win situation.

"The debacle should drive home to the Tigers the futility of exercising the military option. After 14 years of war, Eelam is no more at hand than it was in the early '70s when Prabhakaran cut his teeth as a rebellious tiger cub," the newspaper said.
Velupillai Prabhakaran is the LTTE's leader.
But political analysts said the paper, which usually reflects the thinking of the government, was misreading the situation and that recent losses were unlikely to force rebels into negotiation.

"There is confusion on part of the government media. They are misunderstanding the Tigers, they are not getting the strategic picture correctly," said Dayan Jayatilleka, editor of the monthly Lanka Guardian magazine.
"Prabhakaran may not see 100 rebels dead as defeat. They have been successfully hacking at the rear of the military column, stalling its advance," Jayatilleka told Reuters.
Sri Lankan troops launched a major offensive in May against the LTTE to open a strategic northern highway to link Jaffna peninsula with the rest of the island.
The offensive slowed down after two fierce counter-attacks on the military's rear in June. Fighting escalated last week when rebels mounted another assault on the military.
The LTTE are fighting for a separate homeland, or Eelam, for minority Tamils in Sri Lanka's north and east.
The government says more than 50,000 people have been killed since the war began in 1983. The LTTE put the toll higher.

"In as much as the Tigers are resolute in their destructive course, the armed forces are determined to keep Sri Lanka intact and whole. Given these circumstances it is highly unlikely that the war will yield any benefit for the Tigers," the Daily News said. "They would do well to enter the negotiating process."

Political analyst Paikisothy Saravanamuttu said government media was likely to make similar calls for national reconciliation in a bid to push a peace package that the ruling People's Alliance government unveiled in 1995.

The package, which includes constitutional reforms to devolve more powers to minorities, has been bogged down in a parliamentary select committee over key issues such as the demarcation of new provincial councils and the powers to be devolved.

President Chandrika Kumaratunga's government opened peace talks with the LTTE after winning power in 1994, but these broke down after the rebels sank two navy boats in the harbour of the eastern city of Trincomalee in April 1995.

Justice and Constitutional Affairs Minister Gamini Peiris said last month that the government aimed to reduce the LTTE's military power and then implement constitutional reforms from a position of strength.
